gaps.note: All 21 networks. Seven cycles have not produced one test of a build of this checkout. Every on-chain behaviour test of cycle 7 (the stub tests of hyperevm, high-throughput, op-stack-eth and stablecoin-l1, and the adapter runs of core-code-audit-walk-a) ran against the PoolManagers that are deployed today, and the verifier of walk-a asks that the finding say so. The weakness this review looks for is stated to be in this build, so a probe of a deployed contract can show how a network executes a contract and cannot show what the text of src/ does there. Critic check on 2026-11-23, by reading and by a local Python transcription only: I read src/PoolManager.sol, src/ProtocolFees.sol, src/ERC6909.sol, src/ERC6909Claims.sol, src/NoDelegateCall.sol, src/Extsload.sol, src/Exttload.sol, src/types/Currency.sol, BalanceDelta.sol, BeforeSwapDelta.sol, Slot0.sol, PoolId.sol, PoolKey.sol, every library that the PoolManager uses (Pool, Position, Hooks, SwapMath, SqrtPriceMath, TickMath, TickBitmap, BitMath, FullMath, UnsafeMath, LiquidityMath, SafeCast, CustomRevert, ParseBytes, LPFeeLibrary, ProtocolFeeLibrary, Lock, NonzeroDeltaCount, CurrencyDelta, CurrencyReserves) and lib/solmate/src/auth/Owned.sol. I found no statement that is wrong on its own terms. The 20 multipliers of TickMath.getSqrtPriceAtTick each lie within one unit of 2^128 divided by sqrt(1.0001) to the power 2^i, the function returns MIN_SQRT_PRICE and MAX_SQRT_PRICE at the two end ticks, getTickAtSqrtPrice inverts it on 20,006 ticks at the price and one below it, and both BitMath lookups return the right bit for every position (cycles/007/critic.work/tickmath_bitmath_check.py and its output). The statements whose effect depends on the chain and on nothing in the text are few: the value CALL at src/types/Currency.sol:48, the token call without a code check at lines 64 to 74, SELFBALANCE at line 92, the credit of msg.value at src/PoolManager.sol:354, the guard at line 356 that looks at msg.value only, sync without a lock at lines 279 to 288, the exemption of address(0) at src/ProtocolFees.sol:49, and the four transient stores. Leads L-016, L-232, L-449 and L-483 still wait for a compiler, and no unit in this environment can answer them. I found no rerun of tools/probe.py in the directories of cycles 4 to 7, although README.md asks for one every fourth cycle.

All 21 networks. tools/plan.py line 57 gives a unit in deepen mode the lenses L1 to L4 only, and every unit has been in deepen mode since cycle 2. The cells for L5 and L6 therefore stand at depth 2 with lastCycle 1 on every network in state/ledger.json, for the seventh cycle, and the critics of cycles 4, 5 and 6 said so. Nothing in the planner will change this. The eight angles do reach parts of L6 (upcoming forks, exits), which is how op-stack-eth and hyperevm covered forks this cycle, but owner and controller paths, constructor arguments and the cross-chain ownership path have had no second pass on any network.

Ethereum. The reference network was last visited in cycle 2, and chain id 1 appears in nine of the fifteen confirmed medium findings with actor unprivileged. It is the one network of the 21 without the sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub (lead L-209, with Monad and MegaETH now done in another form by the inherited caller sweep of this cycle). No unit has recorded which Ethereum fork is scheduled on 2026-11-23 or whether it adds a transaction type with more than one frame. The cycle 3 item that says no frame style transaction type is live read one block of 2026-11-22.

BNB Smart Chain and Tempo. Jenner and T14 activate on 2026-12-08, fifteen days from this cycle, and neither chain's sweep describes the state after that date. BNB Smart Chain had no unit in cycle 7. The CAS20 behaviour is known from the Chapel testnet and from the master branch. For Tempo the stablecoin unit simulated the ConfigurableAccount precompile with a later block time and read the registered account case from shim.rs only. T14 is due on the Moderato testnet on 2026-11-24 15:00 UTC, so the registered account case can be run on a live testnet from the next cycle on. The unit filed that as a low lead.

Arc. Critic checks on 2026-11-23, read only, by eth_call with state overrides on https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io, which reports arc/v1, at blocks 32,789,346 to 32,789,352 (scripts and output in cycles/007/critic.work: arc_callfrom, arc_nca2, arc_ncc). The clearances for Arc rest on the main branch of arc-node, and these runs test the node itself. First, Multicall3From 0x522fAf9A91c41c443c66765030741e4AaCe147D0: called directly by an account without code, aggregate3 ran the child call with that account as msg.sender. Called by a contract in between, it reverted with the text sender spoofing requires tx.origin as sender. Entered by DELEGATECALL, it reverted with unauthorized caller. Second, the Native Coin Authority 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000000, with a forwarding stub placed at the token address 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 so that a frame has the token as caller: a plain CALL of transfer(PoolManager, sink, 10^12) returned true, which shows the setup reaches the real precompile. The same call sent by DELEGATECALL from a helper that the token frame had called, where the caller is inherited, reverted with Delegate call not allowed. CALLCODE from the helper reverted with Not enabled for native coin transfers, and STATICCALL reverted with State change during static call. Third, Native Coin Control 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000001 with blocklist(PoolManager): the plain call from the token address returned true, the inherited caller by DELEGATECALL reverted with Delegate call not allowed, STATICCALL reverted, and an ordinary account was refused with Not enabled for blocklisting. A contract that the token calls, for example in a signature check, therefore cannot move or block the PoolManager's native balance through these two precompiles on the running node. Not tested: Memo, the addresses 0x1800...02 to 0x1800...07 with the delegated call kinds, and which release tag arc/v1 corresponds to. The public endpoint refuses eth_call with the token address in the from field (Blocked address), which is why the stub was placed at that address.

Tempo. The inherited caller question is closed by one statement of the client, and the planner need not schedule it again for the current release. Critic read on 2026-11-23 of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tempoxyz/tempo/697ea97/crates/precompiles/src/lib.rs lines 320 to 329: the provider returns DelegateCallNotAllowed for every Tempo precompile whenever the destination of the message differs from the call target, which covers DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE for all tokens and all system precompiles before any selector is read. The verifier of stablecoin-l1 read the same lines. The three precompiles on the implicit approval list (address_registry/mod.rs lines 32 to 36) pull tokens from the direct caller only: stablecoin_dex/mod.rs lines 299 to 305 fed by dispatch.rs lines 25 to 64, tip20_channel_reserve/mod.rs lines 215 and 380 to 384, tip_fee_manager/amm.rs lines 239 and 360 to 364, with the list check at tip20/mod.rs line 966. Still open for Tempo: the interpreter revision of the next release (the unit's low lead), and the question of the cycle 5 critic whether a system transaction with sender zero can reach a contract. protocolFeeController is the zero address on Tempo and state/cleared.json holds a zero sender item for every other network with a zero controller and none for chain id 4217.

Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium. The family had no unit in cycle 7, so the inherited caller angle did not run on the three Nitro chains. Critic read on 2026-11-23 of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/precompiles/precompile.go lines 754 to 757: a precompile method that is view or stronger reverts when the acting address differs from the precompile address, so a DELEGATECALL or CALLCODE into an ArbOS precompile reaches pure methods only. That is the stock source at v3.12.4. The live nodes of Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain report the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9 and Elysium reports a local build, and I found no cleared item that ran DELEGATECALL or CALLCODE against the ArbOS precompiles on chain. No ArbOS precompile keeps a token ledger, so the reach of a hit is smaller than on Arc or Tempo. Second critic read, of the report the cycle 6 critic named (https://docs.arbitrum.io/audit-reports/2026_08_07_trail_of_bits_yield_bearing_bridge_summary_report_with_fix_review.pdf): the yield bearing bridge puts the tokens escrowed on the parent chain into an ERC-4626 master vault that the chain owner manages. It changes no balance on the child chain. When the vault has a loss the share formula spreads the loss over depositors, and the report records that as risk accepted. The hazard is that bridged tokens in pools can be worth less than one unit of the escrowed token, and the actor is the chain owner. Nobody checked whether the gateways of Robinhood Chain or of Elysium are of this kind. The Elysium hook 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec with 104,615 pools is still unread.

MegaETH. The new finding on forced transactions rests on three things that were not seen on chain: the 1,000,000 gas cap was read from a simulation and from strings in the portal bytecode, the growth rule of a SALT bucket comes from the specification and the repository, and no grown bucket was observed on mainnet. The cleared item that says a removal fits in a forced transaction holds for the PositionManager only. The verifier found 21 live positions under two vault contracts of one code (0x5f16b71cc05b146d73e181354b1c8ac89fc4bbc3 and 0xdc41ab847d922fe4375d7d050f518480634ff0e9) whose only recorded removals used 1.17 to 3.24 million gas. That item should not be merged as cleared. F-062 stays plausible on the ordering of skipped transactions, the payload builder is closed, and leads L-170, L-176 and L-177 came back inconclusive for the second time.

HyperEVM. F-020 has been plausible since cycle 1 on a rule the operator has not published: which HyperCore record names an AQAv2 treasury address and whether the node tests that address. Lead L-415 came back inconclusive because no pair of transactions in the history shows a stale sync at a transaction boundary, and the official endpoint refuses eth_simulateV1, eth_callMany and debug_traceCallMany. The 22 probes of this cycle show the official node inside one execution. The boundary between two transactions of one block is still shown by the third party archive client alone.

OP Stack chains with ETH gas. Lagoon is unscheduled and the eight interop predeploy slots are empty on OP Mainnet, Unichain and both Sepolia networks, so lead L-352 cannot be answered before 2026-12-10 at the earliest. The OP Mainnet sequencer still reports a build without a version, and two fixes of 2026 (bare RLP deposits, the trie iterator) could not be tied to the builds of OP Mainnet, World Chain, Zora or Base. The behaviour test of the Unichain predeploy (lead L-217) was not in the plan and was not run, for the sixth cycle. The round trip state diff of lead L-306 covers 457 of 690 tokens on World Chain and 70 of 88 on Soneium. The MUPPETS case shows that the cost of a token transfer can grow with a number any account can raise, and no unit has recorded the gas of a transfer from the PoolManager for the pooled tokens of any network.

Celo and X Layer. The family had no unit in cycle 7. The Celo half of leads L-218 and L-086 (the PositionManager and the first Universal Router name the CELO token, which is the native balance, as their wrapped native address, and 88 pools use that address against 18 on address(0)) is unanswered for the seventh cycle. Leads L-306, L-309 and L-321 were handed to two units in this cycle, each answered its own networks and each wrote that the Celo, Soneium or X Layer part belongs to the other, so those parts were attempted by nobody. F-024 stays plausible on whether the builder filter is switched on, and lead L-263 was not taken.

Polygon, BNB Smart Chain and Avalanche. The family had no unit in cycle 7. The question of the cycle 6 critic is open: the Avalanche endpoint executed a 0xef0100 designator as code and failed, so whether the C-Chain accepts set code transactions is unknown and every delegated account test says nothing for chain id 43114. The verifier of core-code-audit-walk-b found 22 Donate events on BNB Smart Chain in 5,000 blocks where the unit's raw file has no count for seven networks, and counts on that chain still need a second log source.

All 21 networks, reach of theme-transfer-side-effects. The charged transfer test ran on the 13,001 currencies that DefiLlama prices. The verifier found token T on BNB Smart Chain (0x4ef42e4cf51cd779e9947db65b629ecd8c92b1da), which charges 3 percent on top, has a DexScreener price and was counted as unpriced. The holder argument trial ran on full currency lists for 17 networks and on priced currencies only for Robinhood Chain (491), World Chain (89) and MegaETH (11). All trials call the token and its implementation, so a migrator, staking or vault contract with a burn role on the token is not seen. The ARGUS route that the verifier derived (a one sided liquidity add on the main pool paid by take, at a cost of 1 percent where the finding says 3) was read from source and was not simulated.

Hooks with transient state. The AGL finding of op-stack-eth shows a hook that keeps one transient value, changes it in afterSwap and never resets it, so the state one party leaves decides whether the next call in the same transaction passes. theme-hook-ledgers ranked hooks by what they hold in storage and in claims, and theme-shared-hooks probed callbacks outside an unlock. No unit searched the most used hooks (ZoraV4CoinHook with 8,189,715 pools on Base, ContentCoinHook, the Clanker and Doppler hooks, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium, 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc on Monad) for TSTORE and asked what a transient value set through one pool does to a call through another pool of the same hook. The AGL sequence itself was read from the hook source and was not simulated.

leads.question: On the first day after Jenner activates on BNB Smart Chain (2026-12-08 02:30 UTC), run one visit that answers L-346, L-418, L-042, L-406 and the Jenner lead of core-code-loose-guards together. For one live CAS20 token, or for the CAS20 address range and 0x70 if token creation is still closed: (a) the sixteen call shapes through a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, (b) transfer, transferFrom, approve and balanceOf with DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE and STATICCALL from a contract that the stub called, with and without value in that frame, (c) sync, a transfer in, settle and take through the deployed PoolManager, including a transfer from the PoolManager to itself and a transfer of zero, (d) every function of core/vm/cas20.go at the activated commit that writes a balance, with who may call it. Does any call by an account without a role change balanceOf(PoolManager), or return success for a transfer that moves nothing or moves more than the amount?
leads.why: The sweeps of this network describe addresses that answer like accounts without code until the fork, and the token logic was read on a testnet and on the master branch. CAS20 is token code inside the node on one of the two networks with the most swaps. A token that acts on an inherited caller, or whose balance at the PoolManager a stranger can raise between sync and settle (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364), would let an ordinary account take pooled funds as soon as a pool holds one.

leads.question: Run the inherited caller test of cycle 7 where it has not run on chain. Place a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address and a second stub as its callee by state override, and from the callee use DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE and STATICCALL as well as CALL, once without value and once in a frame that received value as the recipient of a native take. Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium: every ArbOS precompile from 0x64 to 0x74, 0xff and 0xa4b05 with one view and one state changing selector each, on the builds that run today. Arc: Memo and the addresses 0x1800...02 to 0x1800...07 (the critic runs of this cycle cover 0x1800...00, 0x1800...01 and Multicall3From). Does any call act with the PoolManager as the account, send a message in its name, or accept a stated value that no balance backs?
leads.why: The PoolManager hands control to caller chosen code with itself as msg.sender in the unlock callback, in every hook call and in every native payout (src/PoolManager.sol:110, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134, src/types/Currency.sol:48). The angle ran on Monad, MegaETH and HyperEVM in cycle 7, on Base and Tempo tokens in cycle 6, and on two Arc precompiles in the critic checks. For the Nitro chains the rejection rests on precompiles/precompile.go lines 754 to 757 at v3.12.4, while Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain run the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9 and Elysium a local build. The ArbOS precompiles hold no token balances, so the likely worst case is a message or withdrawal that names the PoolManager as sender.

leads.question: For each network whose block producer is closed source or reports no version (HyperEVM, MegaETH, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, OP Mainnet), find one mined transaction in which a call frame that had entered PoolManager.unlock reverted and a later frame of the same transaction completed an unlock, for example an on-chain quote by revert followed by the swap. Read it with debug_traceTransaction where an endpoint serves it, or from the receipt together with a replay of the failed inner call. Does such a transaction exist on each of the five, and did the later unlock succeed?
leads.why: The rollback of transient writes with a reverted frame is shown on these networks by RPC nodes and third party clients. A mined transaction of this shape is evidence from the node that produced the block: had the unlock flag survived the reverted frame, the later unlock would have reverted with AlreadyUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:105, src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27). A producer that keeps transient writes of a reverted frame would let a caller keep a settle credit whose payment was rolled back (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41). The expected answer is that all five behave as Ethereum does, and the test replaces an assumption with an observation.

leads.question: Finish the delegated account test on the natively implemented addresses that cycles 6 and 7 did not cover: give an account an EIP-7702 designator that points at each HyperEVM read precompile 0x0800 to 0x0814, at each ArbOS precompile, and at the Arc precompiles 0x1800...00 to 0x1800...07, by state override, and call that account from the PoolManager address with transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address), empty calldata with value and one hook selector. Does the node run the native logic, and if so under which address and which caller?
leads.why: Cycle 6 ran this for tokens on Base, Tempo, Arc, Celo and the Chapel testnet, and cycle 7 for Monad and MegaETH, with four different answers (undefined opcode, empty success, a revert of the proxy, a failed call). A node that ran native logic for a delegated account would give an ordinary account a second address for one piece of chain state. The face walks show that a second address for one balance gives no gain by itself, so the expected result is a clearance.

leads.question: For the ten most used hooks of each of these networks (start with ZoraV4CoinHook 0xc8d077444625eb300a427a6dfb2b1dbf9b159040, ContentCoinHook 0x9ea932730a7787000042e34390b8e435dd839040 and ClankerHookStaticFeeV2 0xb429d62f8f3bffb98cdb9569533ea23bf0ba28cc on Base, 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium and 0x94f802a9efe4dd542fdbd77a25d9e69a6dc828cc on Monad): does the code contain TSTORE, which transient slots does a swap write, are they indexed by pool id, and are they reset before the call returns? For each hook that leaves a value, simulate two swaps in one transaction, the first through a pool that the caller created with the same hook and the second through a pool with other users' liquidity, and compare the second result with the same swap alone. Then repeat with the second swap started from inside the first one, through a token of the caller's pool that calls back when the hook or the PoolManager moves it.
leads.why: AGL shows a hook whose transient quota survives the unlock and changes the outcome of the next call. initialize accepts any pool that names an existing hook (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142), so the caller controls one of the two pools. If a hook with return delta flags reads an amount or a fee from a transient slot that another pool wrote, the caller can move the delta that the PoolManager books to the second pool's swapper or to the hook (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:285-315). The loss would fall on users of a pool whose hook the attacker did not write.

leads.question: Which Ethereum fork is active and which is scheduled on mainnet on the day of the visit (eth_config on an endpoint that serves it, the fork list of the execution specifications, the meta EIP of the next fork)? Does the scheduled fork add a transaction type whose parts run with different senders or roles, and does its specification say whether transient storage is cleared between those parts? Run the sixteen shape sweep through a forwarding stub on Ethereum, which is the reference for every other sweep.
leads.why: The reference network was last visited in cycle 2. A transaction type with several frames would put one party's leftover sync(X) in front of another party's native settle inside one transaction without any contract carrier (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 356, F-014 and F-071), and every OP Stack and Nitro chain adopts Ethereum transaction types some months later.

leads.question: At commit 697ea97 of tempoxyz/tempo, which system transactions does the block executor accept: with which sender, which targets and which input, and what does it do with a transaction whose sender is the zero address and whose target is an ordinary contract? Can a type 0x76 transaction, a fee payer signature or a keychain signature recover to the zero address?
leads.why: protocolFeeController is the zero address on Tempo, and setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees test msg.sender against that value and nothing else (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36 and 48). The cycle 5 critic found no cleared item for this network. An account that could call as the zero address could set the protocol fee to 1,000 pips per direction on every pool and withdraw what accrues. If only a block proposer can place such a transaction the actor is operator.

leads.question: F-062, the one fact: when the MegaETH sequencer skips a transaction because the block has reached 1,000 new state entries, does that transaction run ahead of transactions that arrived later, and is there a limit on queued state growth per sender? Look for a block whose later mini-blocks are empty after a transaction with close to 1,000 new entries and read the first mini-block of the next block, or ask the operator. This merges L-170, L-176, L-177 and the new lead of high-throughput.
leads.why: The finding is plausible for the fourth cycle on this fact. If skipped transactions keep their place, a paid queue delays every later transaction by its length, which together with the forced route cap of this cycle would be a paid delay of exits by an ordinary account. If they do not, the finding is refuted.

leads.question: F-020, the one fact: which HyperCore record names an AQAv2 treasury address and the token that is moved out of it (a validator vote, an undocumented deployer action, or a getter of the linked CoreDepositWallet 0x6b9e773128f453f5c2c60935ee2de2cbc5390a24 read at run time), and does the node accept an address with code in that role? Read the explorer block details between HyperCore block 1,020,511,746 and the first treasury system transaction on 2026-06-12 for an entry that contains 0xc20699185c15D0a2fD65779BB5d69f5b0B113c00. This merges L-065, L-116, L-276, L-323, L-422 and the two new leads of this cycle.
leads.why: The finding has been plausible since cycle 1. The answer decides who the privileged actor is (the validator set, a deployer, or whoever can upgrade the linked contract). It does not open a path for an ordinary account.

leads.question: F-024, the one fact: is the risk control filter of the X Layer block builder switched on for the mainnet sequencer? Take the observation that lead L-263 names. Also answer the X Layer and Soneium parts of L-321 that no unit attempted: by which rule does an address enter the X Layer TxBlacklist and the Soneium restricted list, and can an ordinary account cause an entry for the PoolManager or for a pooled token?
leads.why: F-024 has been plausible since cycle 1 on this flag, and the family did not run in cycle 7. A list that gains entries from observed behaviour would let an ordinary account stop other users' exits, which is why the second half is asked. On Arc the same question was answered this cycle: entries come from named denylisters only.

leads.question: Do the parent chain token gateways of Robinhood Chain (on Ethereum) and of Elysium (on HyperEVM) answer the selector of outboundTransferCustomRefundWithSlippageTolerance, and do they name a master vault? If so, which tokens that the PoolManager holds are bridged through it, what is the vault's share price today, and who holds the vault roles?
leads.why: The yield bearing bridge reviewed by Trail of Bits in August 2026 routes every deposit through an ERC-4626 vault once a chain owner deploys it, and a loss in the vault is spread over depositors at withdrawal, which the report records as accepted. Bridged tokens in pools would then be redeemable for less than their face amount. The actor is the chain owner, so this is recorded for reference.

leads.question: What was the lowest base fee on Arc in the last 1,000,000 blocks (eth_feeHistory), which parameter sets the 20 gwei floor, and who can change it? At which gas price does the rounding gain of one settle on the token face (less than 10^12 wei) exceed the cost of the value call that forces the wei in (at least 9,000 gas)?
leads.why: The clearance of the 12 digit truncation rests on the cost of gas and no longer on a missing path, since this cycle showed that a self destruct delivers native value to the PoolManager. The break even price is about 0.11 gwei. The floor is cited from the documentation page and was not read from chain or from the client.

leads.question: Celo, carried for the seventh cycle (L-218 and L-086): with WETH9() of the deployed PositionManager and of the first Universal Router equal to the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438, simulate through each contract a mint and a full removal on one of the 88 pools that use the CELO token address and on one of the 18 pools that use address(0), with wrap, unwrap, sweep and take actions. Which actions revert, and does any path leave native value or CELO in the contract where the next caller can sweep it?
leads.why: Celo is the one network where the ERC-20 face of the native asset can be paid out by take, and most native liquidity there sits under the face. Ordinary users reach the PoolManager through these two contracts. A path that strands a user's native value in the periphery would be a loss for users who did nothing unusual, and no unit has run it in seven cycles.

leads.question: For each network, take the 200 pooled currencies with the largest priced balance at the PoolManager and measure the gas of transfer(fresh address, 1) from the PoolManager by eth_estimateGas with the from field set. Which tokens need more than 1,000,000 gas, and for which of them does the cost grow with a count that any account can raise (holders, checkpoints, registered recipients, snapshots)? Compare with the gas cap of one transaction on that network.
leads.why: MUPPETS on World Chain needs 4.55 million gas per transfer and 14,143 more per holder, and it stops moving near 1,210 holders under the cap of 16,777,216 gas. That token is in no pool. The same pattern in a pooled token would let any account stop every take of it by creating holders, and no test of earlier cycles recorded gas. op-stack-eth wrote this lead for its seven chains. Every network has a gas cap per transaction or per block, so the question holds for the others too.
